pll-synthesizer-001.question: Which correctly describes the combination of a phase-frequency detector (PFD) and a charge pump used in a PLL?
choices: It detects not only phase difference but also frequency difference, so it can pull the VCO in the right direction even when its frequency is far off, and because the loop-filter capacitor integrates the charge-pump current, the phase error at lock is ideally 0
Like a multiplier (mixer) phase detector, its output is proportional to the sine of the phase difference, so it cannot lock when the frequency is far off
Its output is a DC voltage proportional to the phase difference with no pulses, so no reference spurs arise at all
pll-synthesizer-001.explanation: A PFD compares the edges of the reference and the divided VCO signal and, depending on which arrives first, outputs an UP or DN pulse as wide as the time difference between the edges. When the frequencies differ, one kind of pulse keeps appearing, so the frequency difference is also detected, and the VCO can be pulled in the right direction even from an unlocked state. The charge pump sources or sinks a constant current only during the pulses, and the loop-filter capacitor integrates it, so together with the VCO there are two integrations, making a type II PLL whose phase error at lock is ideally 0. A sinusoidal output that cannot pull in large frequency differences is a property of the multiplier type. The PFD output is pulsed, so the control voltage ripples slightly at the comparison period, which causes reference spurs.

pll-synthesizer-002.question: A pulse-swallow divider uses a 32/33 dual-modulus prescaler, a program counter B = 75 and a swallow counter A = 10. In each cycle the prescaler first divides by 33 for A counts and then by 32 for the remaining B − A counts. With a phase comparison frequency of 1 MHz, what is the output frequency of the locked PLL?
choices: 2400 MHz
2410 MHz
2730 MHz
pll-synthesizer-002.explanation: The overall division ratio is N = 33A + 32(B − A) = 32B + A = 32 × 75 + 10 = 2410, so the output is 2410 × 1 MHz = 2410 MHz. 2400 MHz is the value 32 × 75 with the swallow counter's contribution forgotten. 2730 MHz is the error of adding the A counts of division by 33 to B counts of division by 32, giving 33A + 32B. Each step of A changes N by 1, so the output can be tuned in steps equal to the 1 MHz comparison frequency. Only the prescaler handles the fast division, and the counters need only run at 1/32 of the frequency. However, A ≤ B is required, so N can be chosen continuously only in the range N ≥ 32 × 31 = 992.

pll-synthesizer-003.question: In a charge-pump PLL, if the loop filter is a single capacitor, the loop does not operate stably. Which combination of reason and common remedy is correct?
choices: A capacitor alone gives too little loop gain, so the capacitance is increased to raise the gain
The capacitor does not pass DC, so the VCO control voltage returns to 0. A resistor alone is used instead of the capacitor

The charge pump with the capacitor is one integration and the VCO, which integrates frequency into phase, is another, so the phase of the loop gain is −180° and there is no phase margin. A resistor is placed in series with the capacitor to create a zero and bring the phase back
pll-synthesizer-003.explanation: Turning the charge-pump current into a voltage with a capacitor makes that voltage the integral of the current. The VCO changes frequency with voltage, and phase is the integral of frequency, so another integration enters here. With two integrations, the phase of the loop gain is −180° at all frequencies, there is no phase margin, and the loop cannot operate stably. Placing a resistor in series with the capacitor creates a zero above which the phase recovers, securing phase margin near the loop bandwidth. To suppress the voltage jumps caused by pulsed current through the resistor, a small capacitor is often added in parallel. Increasing the capacitance does not change the phase. With a resistor alone, one integration is lost and a phase error remains when the frequency is changed.

pll-synthesizer-004.question: Which correctly describes the dead zone of a PFD and charge pump?
choices: When the phase difference is very small, the UP and DN pulses are too short for the charge pump to deliver its current, creating a range in which the phase difference cannot be detected. It is avoided by turning UP and DN on simultaneously for a short time every cycle
The range in which the VCO frequency is at the end of its tuning range, so the frequency no longer changes however the control voltage is varied
The range of frequencies in which the phase noise rises because of thermal noise from the loop-filter resistor
pll-synthesizer-004.explanation: When the phase difference is very small, the width of the UP or DN pulses from the PFD becomes shorter than the rise times of the logic and switches, and the charge pump cannot deliver its full current. This creates a dead zone in which the loop gain for small phase differences is nearly 0, and the phase wanders uncontrolled within it, increasing close-in phase noise and spurs. As a remedy, a delay is added to the PFD reset so that, even in lock, UP and DN are both on simultaneously for a short time every cycle. If the UP and DN currents are mismatched, this simultaneous-on time produces a control-voltage ripple every cycle, so it is set as a trade-off against reference spurs. The end of the VCO tuning range and resistor thermal noise are separate issues.

pll-synthesizer-005.question: In a charge-pump PLL, the feedback division ratio N was doubled to double the output frequency, with the loop-filter components and the VCO sensitivity Kvco unchanged. To keep the loop bandwidth the same as before, what should be done to the charge-pump current Icp? Assume the open-loop gain is proportional to Icp·Kvco/N.
choices: Multiply it by √2
Double it
Halve it
pll-synthesizer-005.explanation: The open-loop gain takes the form of the product of the charge-pump current Icp, the loop-filter impedance and the VCO sensitivity Kvco, divided by the division ratio N. Doubling N halves the gain, narrowing the loop bandwidth and moving it away from the frequency where the phase margin peaks. Doubling Icp keeps Icp/N the same as before, restoring both the bandwidth and the phase margin without changing the loop-filter components. Multiplying by √2 comes from noting that the natural angular frequency of a second-order loop, ωn ∝ √(Icp·Kvco/(NC)), falls to 1/√2 and assuming Icp should also be raised by √2; in fact restoring ωn also requires doubling Icp. Halving it makes the gain 1/4 of the original. Synthesizers covering a wide range switch Icp to match N.

pll-synthesizer-006.question: When the loop bandwidth of a PLL is widened, which statement about the output phase noise is correct?
choices: The wider the loop bandwidth, the lower the phase noise at every offset frequency
The VCO phase noise appears at the output in low-pass form through the loop, so widening the loop bandwidth increases the VCO noise out to wider offsets
The VCO phase noise is suppressed out to wider offsets, but the noise of the reference, phase detector and charge pump, multiplied by N, appears at the output out to wider offsets
pll-synthesizer-006.explanation: A PLL acts as a low-pass filter for the noise of the reference, phase detector, charge pump and divider, and inside the loop bandwidth this noise appears at the output multiplied by 20 log₁₀ N. For VCO noise, on the other hand, it acts as a high-pass filter: inside the loop bandwidth the loop suppresses it, and outside it the VCO's own noise appears. Widening the loop bandwidth extends the range over which VCO noise is suppressed, but also extends the range over which the multiplied reference-side noise appears. So when the integrated phase noise (jitter) is to be minimized, a guide is to set the loop bandwidth near the offset where the two noises, referred to the output, cross. The claim that it falls everywhere is wrong, and VCO noise passing in low-pass form has the direction reversed.

pll-synthesizer-007.question: What happens when the phase margin of a PLL loop is reduced from the usual 45–60° or so to about 20°?
choices: A peak appears in the closed-loop response, the phase noise rises near the edge of the loop bandwidth, and the response when switching frequency also rings, lengthening the time to settle
The response becomes faster and the loop locks in the shortest time with no overshoot
The phase margin determines only the size of reference spurs and does not affect phase noise or lock time
pll-synthesizer-007.explanation: With a small phase margin, the closed-loop transfer function has a peak near the loop bandwidth. This peak appears both in the low-pass characteristic that passes reference-side noise to the output and in the high-pass characteristic that suppresses VCO noise, so the phase noise near the edge of the loop bandwidth rises and the integrated jitter increases. In the time response it becomes a lightly damped oscillation (ringing), and the time to settle within the allowed error after a frequency switch actually becomes longer. If component variation or changes in Kvco reduce the phase margin further, there is also a risk of oscillation. Locking in the shortest time without overshoot is the reverse. The phase margin directly affects not only spurs but also phase noise and lock time.

pll-synthesizer-008.question: The in-band phase noise of a PLL is estimated using L1Hz, the noise normalized to 1 Hz that expresses the performance of the phase detector and charge pump, as L = L1Hz + 10 log₁₀ fpfd + 20 log₁₀ N, where fpfd is the comparison frequency in Hz. With L1Hz = −220 dBc/Hz, fpfd = 10 MHz and an output of 2.4 GHz, which is closest to the in-band phase noise?
choices: About −126 dBc/Hz
About −102 dBc/Hz
About −172 dBc/Hz
pll-synthesizer-008.explanation: The division ratio is N = 2.4 GHz/10 MHz = 240, so 20 log₁₀ 240 ≈ 47.6 dB and 10 log₁₀ 10⁷ = 70 dB, giving L = −220 + 70 + 47.6 ≈ −102.4 dBc/Hz. About −126 dBc/Hz is the error of taking the division-ratio term as 10 log₁₀ N ≈ 23.8 dB; multiplying the frequency by N also multiplies the amplitude of the phase fluctuation by N, so the power grows by N². About −172 dBc/Hz drops the comparison-frequency term. Raising the comparison frequency with the output unchanged reduces 20 log₁₀ N while increasing 10 log₁₀ fpfd, so the net effect is a 10 dB improvement for every tenfold increase in the comparison frequency. This is one of the advantages of fractional-N.

pll-synthesizer-009.question: The single-sideband phase noise L(f) of an output at f₀ = 1 GHz is flat at −100 dBc/Hz from 1 kHz to 1 MHz offset and negligible outside that range. Taking the rms phase fluctuation as σφ = √(2∫L(f)df) (L as a linear value) and the rms jitter as σt = σφ/(2πf₀), which is closest to the jitter? Treat the integration width as about 1 MHz.
choices: About 2.3 ps
About 1.6 ps
About 14 ps
pll-synthesizer-009.explanation: The linear value of L(f) is 10⁻¹⁰/Hz, and integrating over a width of about 1 MHz gives 10⁻⁴, that is, −40 dBc. Doubling to combine both sidebands gives 2×10⁻⁴ rad², so σφ = √(2×10⁻⁴) ≈ 0.0141 rad. Converting to time gives σt = 0.0141/(2π × 10⁹) ≈ 2.25×10⁻¹² s, about 2.3 ps. About 1.6 ps is the value from integrating only one sideband and forgetting the factor of 2. About 14 ps is the error of forgetting to divide by 2π, confusing radians with a fraction of the period. Jitter changes with the integration range, so in communication standards and ADC clocks it is compared with the integration range stated. ADC clock jitter sets the upper limit of the SNR when sampling high-frequency inputs.

pll-synthesizer-010.question: In an integer-N PLL, the VCO control voltage ripples as a sine wave of 10 µV amplitude (peak) at the 1 MHz comparison period. With a VCO sensitivity of Kvco = 50 MHz/V, which is closest to the level of the reference spurs appearing ±1 MHz from the output? In narrowband FM, take the amplitude of each sideband as β/2 of the carrier, where β is the modulation index.
choices: About −36 dBc
About −66 dBc
About −72 dBc
pll-synthesizer-010.explanation: The amplitude of the frequency deviation is Δf = Kvco × 10 µV = 50×10⁶ × 10×10⁻⁶ = 500 Hz, and the modulation index is β = Δf/fm = 500/10⁶ = 5×10⁻⁴. The amplitude of each sideband is β/2 = 2.5×10⁻⁴ times the carrier, so the power ratio is 20 log₁₀(2.5×10⁻⁴) ≈ −72 dBc. About −66 dBc is the value with the 1/2 forgotten, taking β itself as the sideband amplitude. About −36 dBc is the error of converting the amplitude ratio to dB with 10 log. The larger Kvco and the lower the comparison frequency, the larger the spurs. For this reason, poles are added to the loop filter to attenuate the comparison-frequency component, and mismatch and leakage in the charge-pump currents are reduced.

pll-synthesizer-011.question: In an integer-N PLL, which combination of main cause and remedy is correct for the reference spurs that appear at the comparison frequency away from the output?
choices: They are caused by the second harmonic of the VCO and disappear if a low-pass filter is placed at the VCO output

They are caused by the control voltage rippling every comparison period because of mismatch between the UP and DN currents of the charge pump, leakage current, the simultaneous-on time used to avoid the dead zone and so on, and they are attenuated by adding poles to the loop filter. However, narrowing the loop bandwidth too much worsens lock time and phase margin
They are caused by the phase noise of the reference crystal oscillator, and the lower the comparison frequency, the smaller the spurs
pll-synthesizer-011.explanation: Even in lock, the charge pump sources and sinks short pulses of current at every comparison. Any slight mismatch between the UP and DN currents, leakage current from switches and capacitors, or simultaneous-on time used to avoid the dead zone makes current flow within each period even if the average is 0, so the control voltage ripples at the comparison frequency. This frequency-modulates the VCO and creates spurs at ±fpfd. The remedies are to add RC poles to the loop filter to attenuate the comparison-frequency component, and to improve current matching and reduce leakage. Narrowing the bandwidth reduces the spurs, but it is a trade-off against lock time and phase margin. Harmonics appear at integer multiples of the carrier and are a separate matter. Lowering the comparison frequency brings the spurs closer to the loop bandwidth, making them harder to suppress.

pll-synthesizer-012.question: In a fractional-N PLL, which correctly describes the purpose of controlling the division-ratio switching with a ΔΣ modulator, and the points to watch?
choices: It turns the phase error from switching the division ratio into noise that grows at higher offsets, instead of periodic spurs, and removes it with the loop's low-pass characteristic. Higher-order ΔΣ makes the noise at far offsets rise steeply, so the loop-filter order and bandwidth must match it, and the phase detector and charge pump must also be highly linear
The ΔΣ modulator completely cancels the switching error, so however wide the loop bandwidth is made, the phase noise outside the band does not increase
Using a ΔΣ modulator fixes the division ratio to an integer, so the output frequency step equals the comparison frequency
pll-synthesizer-012.explanation: Simply switching the division ratio periodically between N and N + 1 makes the average a fraction, but the phase error repeats with a period set by the fractional part, producing large spurs. When a ΔΣ modulator moves the division ratio among values such as N − 1, N, N + 1 and N + 2, this error turns into noise that is small at low offsets and larger at high offsets (noise shaping). The PLL is low-pass for reference-side noise, so the noise above the loop bandwidth is attenuated by the loop filter. However, with higher-order ΔΣ the noise at far offsets rises steeply, so a loop filter of matching order is needed. If the phase detector or charge pump is nonlinear, high-frequency noise mixes together and folds down to low offsets, increasing in-band noise and spurs.

pll-synthesizer-013.question: In a fractional-N PLL with comparison frequency fpfd = 50 MHz, the output is set to 2450.2 MHz. Generating the output very close to an integer multiple of the comparison frequency (2450 MHz) tends to produce integer-boundary spurs. Which is closest to the offset from the output at which this spur appears?
choices: 50 MHz
49.8 MHz
200 kHz
pll-synthesizer-013.explanation: The division ratio is 2450.2/50 = 49.004, with a fractional part of 0.004. The integer multiple of the comparison frequency closest to the output is 49 × 50 = 2450 MHz, and the spur appears at the difference from the output, 0.2 MHz = 200 kHz. It is a difference product formed when the VCO output and harmonics of the comparison frequency or the reference signal mix inside the circuit, and it has the same value as fractional part × fpfd = 0.004 × 50 MHz. When the offset is smaller than the loop bandwidth, the loop does not attenuate it and it appears at the output as is, which makes it especially troublesome. 49.8 MHz confuses it with the difference from the integer multiple on the other side, 2500 MHz. 50 MHz is the position of the reference spur in integer-N operation. One remedy is to change the comparison frequency so the output moves away from integer multiples.

pll-synthesizer-014.question: In a second-order PLL, the time for the error to settle within 1 kHz after a 10 MHz frequency switch is estimated as t ≈ ln(Δf/ftol)/(ζωn), where Δf is the size of the switch and ftol is the allowed error. With damping factor ζ = 0.7 and natural frequency fn = 20 kHz (ωn = 2πfn), which is closest to t?
choices: About 660 µs
About 105 µs
About 45 µs
pll-synthesizer-014.explanation: Δf/ftol = 10 MHz/1 kHz = 10⁴, and ln 10⁴ ≈ 9.21. ωn = 2π × 20×10³ ≈ 1.26×10⁵ rad/s and ζωn ≈ 8.8×10⁴ s⁻¹, so t ≈ 9.21/(8.8×10⁴) ≈ 1.05×10⁻⁴ s, about 105 µs. About 660 µs is the value from using fn directly instead of ωn, forgetting the 2π. About 45 µs is the error of using the common logarithm log₁₀ 10⁴ = 4 instead of the natural logarithm. Lock time is roughly inversely proportional to the loop bandwidth and lengthens by ln 10/(ζωn), about 26 µs in this example, for every tenfold tightening of the allowed error. To switch faster, the loop bandwidth is widened, but that is a trade-off against reference-spur attenuation and in-band noise.

pll-synthesizer-015.question: You want to shorten the lock time at each frequency switch without worsening the reference spurs or phase noise after lock. Which commonly used method is correct?
choices: Increase the loop-filter capacitance and keep the loop bandwidth narrow at all times
Lower the comparison frequency and increase the division ratio N

Increase the charge-pump current only during the switch, also switching the loop-filter resistor to widen the bandwidth while keeping the phase margin, then return to the original narrow bandwidth once settled. The VCO band is also calibrated and selected in advance
pll-synthesizer-015.explanation: Lock time is roughly inversely proportional to the loop bandwidth, so widening the bandwidth settles faster, but keeping the bandwidth wide reduces reference-spur attenuation and spreads in-band noise widely. So a method (fast lock) is used in which, only during the frequency switch, the charge-pump current is raised, for example 4 times, and the resistor is switched to 1/2, widening the bandwidth about 2 times while keeping the phase margin, and then returning to normal once settled. Also, dividing a VCO that covers a wide range into many frequency bands and selecting the band digitally before the switch narrows the frequency range the loop must pull in, shortening the time. Increasing the capacitance to narrow the bandwidth and lowering the comparison frequency both slow the lock.
